questions.questionText: Why is resolving merge conflicts considered a normal part of team development in collaborative Git workflows?
options: Because conflicts indicate that multiple team members edited the same part of the code, requiring a decision on which changes to keep
Because Git automatically merges all changes without any need for human intervention
Because conflicts only occur when the repository is corrupted and must be deleted
Because resolving conflicts eliminates the need for branching strategies
questions.correctAnswer: Because conflicts indicate that multiple team members edited the same part of the code, requiring a decision on which changes to keep
questions.explanation: When collaborators modify the same lines or sections of a file, Git cannot automatically decide which version to retain, so a merge conflict is raised. Resolving these conflicts is a routine step in team development because it ensures that the final code reflects the intended combined changes and maintains project integrity.

questions.questionText: Which of the following sequences correctly describes the steps a collaborator must follow to share a repository with another collaborator within an organization?
options: Generate an SSH key, add it to GitHub, clone the repository, and push changes directly to the main branch.
Create a new branch, make changes, commit them, push to the remote repository, and then open a pull request.
Go to Settings > collaborators, click Manage Access, select Add people, send the invitation, and wait for the collaborator to accept the invitation.
Fork the repository, clone your fork, make edits, and submit a pull request to the original repository.
questions.correctAnswer: Go to Settings > collaborators, click Manage Access, select Add people, send the invitation, and wait for the collaborator to accept the invitation.
questions.explanation: The documented steps for a collaborator to share a repository are: navigate to Settings > collaborators, use Manage Access to click Add people, which sends an invitation to the other collaborator; the invited collaborator must then accept the invitation. The other options describe unrelated Git workflows such as branching, SSH setup, or forking, which are not the specific sharing steps.
